title: Glenohumeral Instability
case: Case: A 20-year-old rugby player dislocated his right shoulder 3 weeks ago and it was reduced in hospital. He now has apprehension when the arm is abducted and rotated outward, and the relocation test reduces it. Sensation over the lateral upper arm is normal and the deltoid contracts well. He wants to return to rugby in 6 weeks.

Working diagnosis: anterior glenohumeral instability after traumatic dislocation. Plan: rehabilitation with progressive strengthening and control, avoid forced external rotation positions, and an early orthopaedic discussion about the risk of recurrence in a young contact athlete. Set return criteria rather than a fixed date.

differentials.name: AC joint injury
differentials.key: Pain on top of the shoulder

differentials.name: Axillary nerve injury
differentials.key: Numbness over the lateral arm, deltoid weakness

qa: Why is pain alone not a positive apprehension test? The test is meant to reproduce the feeling of impending slipping. Pain can come from many structures and does not identify instability.
Why do we check the deltoid and lateral arm sensation after a dislocation? The axillary nerve can be injured, and the finding changes referral urgency and rehabilitation.
Why not stretch the capsule in MDI? The problem is too much looseness, so stretching is more likely to worsen it. Strength and control are the target.
A 55-year-old cannot lift the arm after dislocation. What is suspected? A rotator cuff tear, so refer for early imaging.
Why discuss surgery early in this player? Young contact athletes have a high redislocation risk, so the surgeon and patient should discuss the options early [Ref - to verify].

fields.Purpose: Check whether the position of anterior instability provokes the feeling that the shoulder will slip
fields.Patient position: Supine (more secure) or sitting; arm abducted to 90 degrees, elbow bent to 90 degrees
fields.Therapist position: Beside the shoulder; one hand supports the elbow, the other the wrist
fields.Action: Slowly rotate the arm outward (external rotation), stopping at the first sign of apprehension or at end range
fields.Positive: The patient shows or reports apprehension (a feeling that it will come out), and may resist further movement
fields.Negative: No apprehension. Pain alone is not a positive result
fields.Supports: Anterior instability when combined with the history
fields.Limits: Requires the patient's cooperation; low reproducibility if the patient is guarded [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Moving fast; forcing the movement; calling pain alone positive
fields.Next step: If positive, do the relocation test

fields.Purpose: Check whether a posterior force on the humeral head reduces apprehension
fields.Position: Supine, same arm position as E1
fields.Action: At the point where apprehension occurs, apply a gentle posteriorly directed force to the front of the humeral head, then see if the patient can rotate further with less apprehension
fields.Surprise (release) variation: When the posterior force is suddenly released and apprehension returns, the result is reported to be more convincing [Ref - to verify]
fields.Supports: Anterior instability; the combination of apprehension, relocation and release is often used together [Ref - to verify]

fields.Position and action: Supine or sitting, arm about 20 to 30 degrees abduction; compress the head into the socket, then shift it forward and back
fields.Positive: Excessive translation compared with the other side, with symptoms

fields.Position and action: Sitting, arm relaxed at the side; apply a gentle downward pull on the arm
fields.Positive: A visible gap or dimple under the acromion that is larger than the other side; supports inferior laxity, as in MDI

fields.Position and action: 9-point scale of finger, thumb, elbow, knee and trunk flexibility
fields.Positive: Higher scores suggest generalised hypermobility; the threshold varies by population [Ref - to verify]

redFlags.Finding: Visible deformity, cannot move the arm after injury
redFlags.Immediate action: Support the arm in the position of comfort; do not attempt relocation unless trained and permitted; send for imaging and reduction

redFlags.Finding: Numb or pale, cool, pulseless hand; severe swelling
Numbness over the lateral upper arm, weak deltoid
Age over 40 with weakness after a dislocation
Locked shoulder after seizure or electric shock

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: rehabilitation, not manual therapy. Do not stretch or mobilise the capsule of an unstable shoulder. Avoid forcing end-range external rotation. Manual therapy has a small supporting role only (comfort, thoracic mobility).

exercise.Steps: Elbow at side, push into a wall or hand

exercise.Exercise: Banded external and internal rotation at the side; rows; serratus punches
exercise.Steps: Elbow at the side, light band

exercise.Exercise: Scaption, quadruped weight shift, closed-chain loading
Plyometric catches, overhead loading, contact preparation

exerciseNotes: Principle: build the dynamic stability of the cuff and scapular muscles in positions the patient can control, then progress toward the position of instability and sport demands. Programs for atraumatic instability usually follow a long, structured plan [Ref - to verify].
Avoid early: end-range external rotation with abduction (the position of instability), forceful stretches, and unsupervised heavy contact sport.

Return to sport criteria (example): no apprehension, strength and endurance close to the other side, confident sport-specific movements, and agreement with the medical team. Use objective measures where available; no fixed time is stated [Ref - to verify].

modalities.name: Taping or bracing
modalities.comment: Proprioceptive cue or temporary protection in sport; limited evidence [Ref - to verify]

modalityNotes: A sling after a first dislocation is typically short-term; the best position and duration are debated [Ref - to verify]. Follow the treating doctor's instruction.
pathway: Acute deformity or neurovascular signs? Yes: emergency pathway.
History of dislocation or slipping plus apprehension and relocation signs? Yes: working diagnosis is anterior glenohumeral instability.
Generalised laxity, no major injury, symptoms in several directions? Yes: working diagnosis is multidirectional or atraumatic instability; first line is rehabilitation.

Young, active, first-time traumatic dislocation, or recurrent dislocations, or high-demand contact sport? Yes: discuss an orthopaedic opinion early, because surgery may be considered [Ref - to verify].
Acute: refer for reduction and imaging. Protect the shoulder, manage pain, check nerves and vessels.
Early rehabilitation: restore pain-free movement within safe limits, begin isometrics and scapular work.
Strengthening: progress rotator cuff, scapular and trunk strengthening.
